overview: W̱SÁNEĆ people describe themselves as Salt Water People. Their homeland includes the Saanich Peninsula and neighbouring islands and waters. Fishing places, winter villages, language and responsibilities to other living beings connect this history with continuing community life.

periods.title: A writing system supports language teaching
periods.summary: Dave Elliott developed a SENĆOŦEN alphabet, adopted by the Saanich Indian School Board in 1984. Writing supported transmission of a language already carried through generations.

periods.title: A territorial declaration
periods.summary: The Saanich declaration affirmed continuing title and responsibility to the homeland. It expressed the communities’ position rather than marking the beginning of their relationship with the territory.

periods.title: Young people rebuild reef-net practice
periods.summary: Youth worked with Elders and knowledge holders on materials, paddling and net deployment. Repeated trials made the practical challenges of renewing the fishery visible.

items.text: Dave Elliott remembered helping prepare reef-net ropes, floats and stone anchors as a boy. He emphasised the knowledge of tides, wind and rope strength needed to keep equipment in place. A fishing installation depended on careful local judgement, not simply a net.

Elliott explained that willow inner bark supplied strong twine for the reef net. The material’s preparation and strength mattered in fast-moving salt water. His account links plant knowledge on land with equipment used far from shore.

The Council describes families as custodians of particular reef nets and harvesting locations. Fishing was therefore embedded in responsibilities toward places and marine life, as well as in the work of catching and sharing food.

Youth-project coordinator Edna Ellsworth explains that the net guides salmon upward and includes an opening through which some can escape. The design combines capture with provision for fish to continue their journey.

In August 2025, the youth team adjusted weights and successfully positioned its net in the water. The team caught no fish on that outing. The documented achievement was learning how to deploy the equipment, rather than a demonstrated harvest.

Clam gardens use rock walls to retain sediment and create flatter intertidal habitat. Maintaining such a shore involves moving stones and tending the beach. These food-producing places show people actively shaping marine environments.

Recent restoration at Fulford Harbour and other sites brings together wall repair, sediment tending, youth education and laboratory testing of shellfish. Harvests that meet safety requirements are shared with community members, including Elders. This is continuing practical work, not only preservation of old structures.

The account of ĆENŦEḴI, the Sockeye Moon, connects salmon fishing with summer weather, bird calls and ripening strawberries and salmonberries. Its calendar guides related activities through the seasons; its moons do not correspond exactly to modern calendar months.

Catching salmon in the straits before they reached rivers supported exchange with inland peoples. The Council’s seasonal account links this timing to a trading advantage, showing how ecological knowledge shaped economic relationships.

The same account describes pausing fishing for a ceremony when the first sockeye was caught. Songs, prayer and a shared meal acknowledged the salmon. Food gathering and spiritual responsibilities belonged to a connected practice.

ending.text: Colonial fishing restrictions and residential schooling disrupted harvesting and language transmission. W̱SÁNEĆ communities continue to assert responsibilities to their homeland and rebuild fisheries, teaching and ecological care. These are histories of continuing people, not a vanished civilisation.
